analysis.investment_thesis: A tiny ₹75.5 Cr microcap publisher with a 0.31% ROE is earning essentially nothing on shareholder capital — the opposite of the "wonderful business" I seek. At 15.9x P/E, you're paying a full market multiple for a business in a structurally declining industry with no discernible moat.
key_strengths: Promoter holding of 64.78% shows skin in the game
key_risks: ROE of 0.31% is catastrophically below cost of capital (~12-14%)
Print publishing is in secular decline vs. digital media
₹75.5 Cr microcap — illiquid, limited analyst coverage, governance risk
red_flags: ROE of 0.31% indicates capital is being destroyed, not compounded
No evidence of a durable moat in regional publishing
Microcap size makes financial data reliability questionable
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The single most important number here is ROE of 0.31%. I've said for decades that the test of a business is the return it earns on shareholder equity — a company earning one-third of one percent on its capital would be better off liquidating and putting the money in a government bond. Charlie and I look for consistent 15%+ ROE; this is roughly 50x below that threshold. Paying 15.9x earnings for near-zero returns on capital means you're compounding at the ROE, not the earnings yield — this is a value trap.

Beyond the numbers, printing and publication in India faces the same headwinds that crushed newspapers globally: migration to digital, collapsing ad revenue, and rising newsprint costs. A ₹75.5 Cr regional publisher has no pricing power, no network effects, no brand moat that would let it compete with digital-native players. Promoter holding of ~65% is the only mild positive, but owner-alignment cannot fix an economically unattractive business. I'll pass — there is no margin of safety when the underlying business itself cannot earn its cost of capital.
